The trick to getting away with one is integrating an impactor into the chassis of your bot, using the single wheel to spin up to ~3k RPM, then by tracking the rotation angle of the bot as it spins, you speed up a little while the wheel is pointing where you want to go, and slow it down a little when it's pointing the other direction.

By that I mean that, rather than let the LLM do the entire structure, I take the time to create the full hierarchy of abstractions and actors that I want my code to do. I decide, at the UML level, how abstractions will sit and interact — and then I make the LLM implement those gaps.

But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out.

Interesting. Most of the failures I've seen aren't the agent doing something obviously daft, it's a tool call that returns fine but the result shouldn't be trusted. comments.author: scottfalconer

We ran into an interesting side effect of agent performance that we needed to explain in our results to our executive team. In our case we were rolling out an AI support agent that could help resolve customer problems. At the start we had calculated the total time and human cost per support ticket going back a few years. After a few months of running the AI agent, we found that both our time and cost per ticket had increased - but then digging in, the issue was that our overall cost and time had decreased and it was just that the more complicated issues the agent wasn't able to answer were the ones now going to the humans, skewing our per ticket cost up.
So in this case it's not that it was a different failure, it was that a signal that seemed to indicate failure was actually a signal of success.
